days.learn: Multi-stage Dockerfiles, small images, non-root users
days.title: Dockerfile for the API
days.doneWhen: `docker build` produces an API image that runs as a non-root user, answers `/health` on port 8080 with every setting from environment variables, and a second build after changing one `.cs` file restores packages from cache
days.brief:
### Why this matters
"Works on my machine" ends when the machine is an image. A multi-stage build compiles with the full SDK and ships only the small runtime with your published output, so images are smaller and carry no compilers or source. Running as a non-root user limits what an attacker can do after a break-in. Writing a Dockerfile from memory is part of this week's checkpoint. Today's React part packages the web app the same way.

### What you'll build
On a new branch `feature/ship-it`:
- `api/Dockerfile` with stages: `build` (the .NET 10 SDK image), `publish`, and `final` (the ASP.NET Core 10 runtime image)
- Layer caching: copy the `.csproj` files and restore first, then copy the source
- `dotnet publish -c Release` into `/app`
- The final stage running as the non-root user the .NET images provide (`USER $APP_UID`), on port 8080
- A writable uploads folder owned by that user (until Thursday moves files to blob storage)
- `api/.dockerignore` excluding `bin`, `obj`, `.git`, `.env` and test output
- The `docker` ecosystem added to Dependabot (week 18)

### Step by step
1. Sketch the stages and what each copies.
2. Write build and publish. Build once, change one `.cs` file, build again: restore comes from cache.
3. Write the final stage: copy only the published output.
4. Set the user and port; confirm with `docker exec <id> whoami`.
5. Run it with settings as environment variables (`Jwt__SigningKey`, `ConnectionStrings__JobHunt`) pointing at your local SQL Server.
6. Record the image size in the PR.

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
# TODO: copy csproj files keeping folders, restore, copy source, publish to /app
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The final image has no SDK or source
- [ ] It runs as a non-root user
- [ ] All settings come from the environment
- [ ] Restore is cached between builds

### Hints
- `docker history <image>` shows each layer; a secret copied into any layer can leak.
- The .NET SDK can also build images without a Dockerfile; knowing the Dockerfile way makes that easy to read.

### Common mistakes
- `COPY . .` before restore, so every code change re-downloads packages.
- Baking `appsettings.Development.json` or secrets into the image.

### Check your understanding
- What does each stage contribute?
- Why restore before copying the source?
- Why run as non-root, and why port 8080?

days.title: Dockerfile for the web app served by nginx with SPA fallback
days.doneWhen: The web image builds the app with Node and serves `dist` from an unprivileged nginx, a deep link such as `/applications/<id>/notes` reloads without a 404, hashed assets are cached long and `index.html` is not, and the week 18 CSP arrives as a header
days.brief:
### Why this matters
In production there is no Vite dev server: the app is static files, and something must serve them. nginx is small and fast, but a SPA needs one special rule: any unknown path returns `index.html` so React Router can handle it, or every deep link 404s on reload. Caching rules decide whether users get new releases. Today's .NET part builds the API image; tomorrow nginx also proxies to it.

### What you'll build
- `web/Dockerfile`: a Node LTS stage running `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then an unprivileged nginx stage serving `dist`
- `web/nginx.conf` with:
  - `try_files $uri /index.html` for SPA routes
  - long `Cache-Control` with `immutable` for hashed `/assets/`, `no-cache` for `index.html`
  - the week 18 CSP and security headers with `add_header ... always`
- `web/.dockerignore` excluding `node_modules`, `dist` and `.env*`

### Step by step
1. Write the Dockerfile; `npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says.
2. Write a server block serving `dist` with the SPA fallback.
3. Add the cache rules: hashed files forever, the HTML entry never.
4. Paste the CSP text from week 18 into a header.
5. Build and run the image; open a deep link and reload.
6. Check headers in the Network tab.

```nginx
location / {
    try_files $uri /index.html;
}
# TODO: location /assets/ with long immutable caching
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Deep links survive a reload
- [ ] Assets are cached, `index.html` is revalidated
- [ ] The CSP is a response header
- [ ] nginx runs unprivileged

### Hints
- `add_header` in a `location` replaces headers from the outer block; repeat them or use an include file.
- Unprivileged nginx images listen on 8080, like the API.

### Common mistakes
- Caching `index.html`, so users never get the new release.
- A fallback that also catches `/api`, returning HTML to API calls (tomorrow fixes routing).

### Check your understanding
- Why does a SPA need a fallback rule?
- Why cache assets forever but not `index.html`?
- What did the Vite dev server do that nginx must now do?

days.learn: docker compose: services, health checks, volumes
days.title: compose runs the API with SQL Server, Redis and RabbitMQ
days.doneWhen: `docker compose up` starts SQL Server, Redis, RabbitMQ, the SMTP catcher and the API in order using health checks, the API answers `/health/ready` healthy, and `docker compose down -v` followed by `up` works from scratch with only `.env` filled in

learnLinks.label: Docker Docs: Environment variables in Compose

days.brief:
### Why this matters
JobHunt now depends on four services. A new developer (or a reviewer) should run one command, not follow ten setup steps. Compose describes the whole stack, and health checks make services wait for each other instead of crashing at start-up. Tomorrow's migrator and nginx plug into this file. Today's React part routes traffic to the API through nginx.

### What you'll build
- `compose.yaml` at the repo root with `sqlserver`, `redis`, `rabbitmq` (management image), `mailpit` (or your catcher) and `api`
- Health checks: `sqlcmd` for SQL Server, `redis-cli ping`, `rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping`, and the API's `/health/ready` (week 19)
- `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`
- Named volumes for SQL Server and RabbitMQ data
- Settings from `.env` (week 18's `.env.example`), never in `compose.yaml`; services reached by name (`sqlserver`, `redis`), not `localhost`
- Only tool UIs publishing ports for now; tomorrow `web` becomes the single entry point

### Step by step
1. Write the infrastructure services and get each healthy with `docker compose ps`.
2. Add the API with `build: ./api` and its environment.
3. Add `depends_on` conditions.
4. Apply migrations by hand once for today; Wednesday adds the migrator.
5. Read `docker compose logs -f api` until start-up is clean.
6. Run `down -v` and `up` again from scratch.

```yaml
api:
  build: ./api
  env_file: .env
  depends_on:
    sqlserver: { condition: service_healthy }
    # TODO: redis, rabbitmq
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One command starts the stack
- [ ] Services wait for healthy dependencies
- [ ] No secrets in `compose.yaml`
- [ ] Data survives `down` without `-v`

### Hints
- SQL Server takes a while to start; give its health check a start period.
- Week 18's trusted proxy list will need the Compose network range tomorrow.

### Common mistakes
- `localhost` in connection strings inside containers.
- `depends_on` without a condition, which only orders start, not readiness.

### Check your understanding
- Why health checks and not just start order?
- How do services find each other?
- What does `-v` delete?

days.learn: nginx as a reverse proxy, including WebSockets
days.title: nginx routes /api and /hubs to the API (replacing the Vite proxy)
days.doneWhen: With `web` and `api` in Compose, the app works at one URL through nginx: `/api` calls, login refresh with the httpOnly cookie, live updates over a WebSocket on `/hubs`, and a 5 MB upload, while the API sees real client IPs through forwarded headers from nginx only
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Since week 3 the Vite proxy has quietly made everything same-origin: cookies just worked, CORS was not needed, and week 15's WebSocket went through untouched. In production nginx takes that job. Missing one piece (the WebSocket upgrade headers, the body size limit, forwarded headers) breaks a feature only in production. This puts today's .NET Compose stack behind one entry point.

### What you'll build
- `location /api/` and `location /hubs/` in `nginx.conf` proxying to `http://api:8080`
- For `/hubs`: HTTP/1.1 and the `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers, plus a longer read timeout
- `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` set on both locations
- `client_max_body_size` slightly above week 14's 5 MB limit
- The API's trusted proxy list (week 18) set to the Compose network, so forwarded headers from nginx are honoured and nobody else's are
- `web` added to `compose.yaml` as the only service publishing a port
- `/hangfire` not routed (Friday decides how admins reach it)

### Step by step
1. List everything the Vite proxy did in weeks 3, 8, 14 and 15; each needs an nginx line or a decision.
2. Add the two locations before the SPA fallback, so API calls never get `index.html`.
3. Add the WebSocket headers and check the Network tab shows status 101 for `/hubs`.
4. Add forwarded headers and set the API's trusted network.
5. Log in, reload (refresh cookie), open two tabs (live updates), upload a file.
6. Check a rate-limited login logs the real client IP, not nginx's.

```nginx
location /hubs/ {
    proxy_pass http://api:8080;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    # TODO: Upgrade and Connection headers, forwarded headers, read timeout
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every feature works through nginx alone
- [ ] `/hubs` uses a WebSocket, not long polling
- [ ] Uploads up to the limit pass
- [ ] Forwarded headers are trusted only from nginx

### Hints
- Same origin through nginx means the refresh cookie and CORS need no changes.
- If live updates fall back to long polling, the upgrade headers are missing.

### Common mistakes
- Putting the SPA fallback first, so `/api` returns HTML.
- Forgetting the body size, so uploads fail with 413 only in production.

### Check your understanding
- What did the Vite proxy do that you now configure?
- Why do WebSockets need special headers?
- Why must the API trust only nginx's forwarded headers?

days.learn: Migrations on deploy: bundles and expand/contract
days.title: EF migration bundle run as a step before the new version starts
days.doneWhen: A `migrator` build target produces an EF Core migrations bundle, a `migrator` Compose service runs it against SQL Server and exits, the API starts only after it completes successfully, and the PR notes describe one expand and contract change
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Calling `Migrate()` at start-up seems easy, until two instances start together and race, or a migration fails halfway through a deploy. A migrations bundle is a single executable that applies pending migrations as a separate step before the new version starts. Expand and contract keeps old and new versions working during the switch. Both are standard answers to "how do you deploy schema changes?". Today's React part makes one web image fit every environment.

### What you'll build
- A `migrator` stage in `api/Dockerfile` running `dotnet ef migrations bundle` into a single executable
- A `migrator` service in `compose.yaml`: built with `target: migrator`, connection string from `.env`, runs once and exits
- The API's `depends_on` waiting for `service_completed_successfully`
- Any start-up `Migrate()` call removed (week 19's E2E reset keeps its own explicit path)
- A note in the PR describing expand and contract with a JobHunt example

### Step by step
1. Read the applying migrations page, sections on bundles and on applying at runtime.
2. Add the stage; the bundle needs the EF tools, so build it in an SDK-based stage.
3. Run the bundle once by hand against your local SQL Server with `--connection`.
4. Add the Compose service and the API's dependency.
5. `down -v`, `up`: the migrator runs, exits 0, then the API starts.
6. Write the expand and contract example: renaming a column as add new, copy, switch code, drop old across releases.

```yaml
migrator:
  build: { context: ./api, target: migrator }
  depends_on:
    sqlserver: { condition: service_healthy }
  # TODO: connection string from .env
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Migrations run as a separate step
- [ ] A failed migration stops the API from starting
- [ ] No start-up `Migrate()` in production code
- [ ] Expand and contract is explained with an example

### Hints
- Friday's pipeline runs the same bundle before rolling out a new revision.
- A bundle is idempotent: it applies only pending migrations.

### Common mistakes
- Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
- Running migrations from every API instance at start-up.

### Check your understanding
- Why a separate step instead of start-up migration?
- What does expand and contract protect against?
- What happens if the migrator fails?

days.learn: Build-time vs run-time configuration for a SPA
days.title: Runtime config file so one image works in every environment
days.doneWhen: The web container writes `/config.json` from environment variables at start-up, the app loads it before rendering and shows the environment name in the footer, and the same image shows "Staging" or "Production" depending only on the environment it runs with

learnLinks.label: Docker Docs: Environment variables in Compose

days.brief:
### Why this matters
`VITE_` variables are baked into the bundle at build time, so a staging build and a production build are different images, and you never quite test what you ship. A small runtime config file, written when the container starts, lets one image run everywhere. Everything secret stays on the server: anything the browser can read is public. Today's .NET part makes the database ready before the app; this makes config ready before render.

### What you'll build
- `RuntimeConfig` type: `environmentName`, `apiBaseUrl` (default `""`, same origin), and one feature flag such as `showDemoBanner`
- A tiny entrypoint script in the web image that writes `/usr/share/nginx/html/config.json` from environment variables before nginx starts
- `index.html` or `main.tsx` fetching `/config.json` before `createRoot(...).render`, with safe defaults if it fails
- `config.json` served with `no-cache`
- Week 3's typed config module reading from runtime config first, then `import.meta.env` for local dev
- A footer showing the environment, and the demo banner behind the flag

### Step by step
1. List every `import.meta.env` use; decide build-time or run-time for each.
2. Write the type and a loader that validates the JSON (Zod is fine).
3. Write the entrypoint script; keep it to a few lines and quote values.
4. Load config before rendering; show nothing secret.
5. Add the cache header for `config.json`.
6. Run the same image twice with different environment values.

```ts
export async function loadRuntimeConfig(): Promise<RuntimeConfig> {
  // TODO: fetch /config.json with no-store, validate, fall back to defaults
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One image works in every environment
- [ ] The app renders with safe defaults if config is missing
- [ ] No secret ever appears in config
- [ ] `config.json` is never cached

### Hints
- Local development keeps using `.env` files; the runtime file only exists in the container.
- Because every API URL is relative, JobHunt barely needs runtime config; that is a good design, not a gap.

### Common mistakes
- Rebuilding the image per environment.
- Putting API keys in runtime config "because it is not in the bundle".

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between build-time and run-time config?
- Why must runtime config hold nothing secret?
- Why load it before rendering?

days.learn: Scaling out statelessly: backplanes, shared keys, file storage
days.title: Checklist for two instances: SignalR backplane, Data Protection keys, blob storage
days.doneWhen: `SCALING.md` lists every piece of in-process state with its fix, and with `docker compose up --scale api=2` a card moved in a tab connected to one instance updates a tab on the other, stats eviction reaches both, the dashboard cookie works on either, and uploads land in Azurite

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: SignalR hosting and scaling
Microsoft Learn: Redis backplane for SignalR

days.brief:
### Why this matters
One instance can keep state in memory; two cannot. With two API instances, a SignalR message sent on instance A never reaches a tab connected to B, an output cache eviction clears only one copy, a cookie protected with A's keys fails on B, and a file saved on A's disk is missing on B. Being able to list these and fix them is exactly this week's checkpoint question.

### What you'll build
- `SCALING.md`: each piece of in-process state, what breaks with two instances, the fix, status
- SignalR Redis backplane (`AddStackExchangeRedis` on the SignalR builder)
- The Redis output cache store, so week 13's per-user tag eviction reaches every instance
- Data Protection keys persisted to Redis or blob storage with one application name, so the week 14 dashboard cookie works anywhere
- `BlobFileStorage : IFileStorage` with `Azure.Storage.Blobs`, chosen by configuration, and Azurite in Compose
- Notes on what stays per instance: rate limit counters (week 13), the event sequencer (week 15, the epoch makes clients resync), the outbox publisher (week 17: needs locked-row skipping or a lease)

### Step by step
1. Grep for singletons, static fields and `IMemoryCache`; write each into the table.
2. Add the backplane and the output cache store, both pointing at Compose's Redis.
3. Persist Data Protection keys and set the application name.
4. Add Azurite to Compose and implement `BlobFileStorage`; week 14 tests should pass with either provider.
5. Scale to two and test each fix with two tabs.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every row in `SCALING.md` has a fix or an accepted limit
- [ ] Live updates cross instances
- [ ] Cookies and cache eviction work on either instance
- [ ] Files are shared storage, not local disk

### Hints
- With several instances, SignalR needs sticky sessions unless clients use WebSockets only and skip negotiation; note your choice.
- Hangfire with SQL Server storage already coordinates several servers.

### Common mistakes
- Testing "scaling" with one instance.
- Forgetting the application name, so instances still cannot read each other's keys.

### Check your understanding
- Why must the API be stateless to scale out?
- What does a backplane do?
- Which state did you accept as per instance, and why?

days.learn: GitHub Actions: jobs, caching, test reports
days.title: CI for the web app: lint, type check, tests, build
days.doneWhen: Every pull request runs a GitHub Actions job for `/web` that installs with an npm cache, lints, type-checks, runs Vitest with a test report, and builds, and a pull request that breaks a test shows a red check

learnLinks.label: GitHub Docs: Building and testing Node.js

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Tests nobody runs protect nothing. Continuous integration runs every check on every pull request, on a clean machine, so "it passed on my laptop" stops being an argument. Caching keeps it fast; a test report makes failures readable without digging through logs. Today's .NET part makes the API scale; this makes every change prove itself.

### What you'll build
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` triggered on pull requests and pushes to main
- A `web` job on `ubuntu-latest` with `defaults.run.working-directory: web`
- `actions/setup-node` with the Node version from `.nvmrc` (or `package.json` engines) and npm caching
- Steps: `npm ci`, lint, `tsc --noEmit`, `vitest run` with a JUnit reporter, `npm run build`
- The test report uploaded as an artifact with `if: always()`, and a short line in the job summary
- A CI badge in the README

### Step by step
1. Read the Node.js guide and the workflow basics: triggers, jobs, steps.
2. Write the job with checkout and setup-node; turn on npm caching.
3. Add the steps in the order a reviewer would care: install, lint, types, tests, build.
4. Configure a JUnit reporter in Vitest and upload the file.
5. Push a branch, open a pull request, watch it run.
6. Break a test on purpose, see the red check, fix it.

```yaml
jobs:
  web:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: web } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      # TODO: setup-node with npm cache, ci, lint, typecheck, test, build
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Runs on every pull request
- [ ] Fails on lint, type or test errors
- [ ] Cached installs are faster than the first run
- [ ] The test report is downloadable

### Hints
- Use `npm ci`, never `npm install`, in CI: it fails if the lock file is out of date.
- Pin actions to a major version; Dependabot (week 18) keeps them current.

### Common mistakes
- Steps that continue after a failure because of `|| true`.
- Caching `node_modules` directly instead of the npm cache.

### Check your understanding
- What does CI prove that local runs do not?
- Why `npm ci`?
- What does caching key on?

days.title: CD to Azure Container Apps (or App Service) with secrets from Key Vault
days.doneWhen: Merging to main builds and pushes both images, runs the migrations bundle, rolls out new revisions with secrets read from Key Vault through a managed identity, runs the week 19 smoke test against the live URL, and the PR "Ship it" is open

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Azure Container Apps overview
Microsoft Learn: Manage secrets in Azure Container Apps
GitHub Docs: OpenID Connect in Azure

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Continuous delivery means every merge to main can reach users without manual steps, and a failed step stops the rollout before users see it. Deploying from a pipeline with no stored cloud passwords (OpenID Connect) and secrets from a vault is how teams ship safely. This closes the .NET side of the PR "Ship it".

### What you'll build
- `.github/workflows/cd.yml` on push to main: build and push images (GitHub Container Registry or Azure Container Registry), run the migrations bundle, update both apps, run `scripts/smoke.sh`
- Azure login with OpenID Connect federated credentials: no cloud secrets in GitHub
- Container Apps: `web` with external ingress, `api` internal behind nginx, a managed identity reading Key Vault (week 18) and blob storage
- Hangfire dashboard off in production, or behind the admin cookie over HTTPS, never public
- The platform's ingress as the trusted proxy for forwarded headers

### Step by step
1. No Azure subscription? Use App Service or any container host; the decisions matter more than the provider.
2. Create resources once (portal or CLI), including SQL, Redis and RabbitMQ, and record them in `DEPLOY.md`.
3. Write the workflow: build, push, migrate, deploy, smoke. Any failure stops the next step.
4. Give the API's managed identity read access to Key Vault; secrets never appear in the workflow.
5. Set API replicas to 2 and repeat Thursday's checks on the live URL.
6. Push and open the PR "Ship it"; merge after today's React part, then watch the first deploy.

```yaml
- name: Migrate database
  run: ./efbundle --connection "${{ steps.conn.outputs.value }}"
# TODO: update the api and web apps, then run the smoke test
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No cloud password or secret stored in GitHub
- [ ] Migrations run before the new revision
- [ ] The smoke test gates the deploy
- [ ] Two API replicas behave correctly

### Hints
- Migrations must be backwards compatible (Wednesday): the old revision runs against the new schema for a while.
- Container Apps keeps the previous revision for quick rollback.

### Common mistakes
- Deploying the API before migrating.
- Long-lived service principal secrets instead of OpenID Connect.

### Check your understanding
- What does OpenID Connect remove from your pipeline?
- Why migrate before rolling out?
- What happens when the smoke test fails?

days.title: CI for the API with coverage thresholds, both required on pull requests
days.doneWhen: The CI workflow also has an `api` job running `dotnet test` with Testcontainers and a merged coverage threshold, Vitest fails below its own thresholds, a ruleset on main requires both checks and a pull request, and PR "Ship it" is merged
days.brief:
### Why this matters
CI that can be skipped is a suggestion. Required checks make "green before merge" a rule, and coverage thresholds stop the slow slide where each pull request adds untested code. This lesson lives in the React lane but covers both apps' gates, since they protect one repository together. It ends the week with the PR "Ship it", together with today's .NET part.

### What you'll build
- An `api` job in `ci.yml`: `actions/setup-dotnet` for .NET 10, NuGet caching, `dotnet build`, `dotnet test` with coverage (Docker is available on Ubuntu runners, so Testcontainers works)
- A .NET coverage threshold that fails the job when merged line coverage drops, using week 11's report or the coverage collector's threshold option
- Vitest `coverage.thresholds` set a little below today's numbers (the week 11 stretch, now enforced)
- Optional: the week 19 E2E job needing both, uploading traces on failure
- A ruleset on main: pull request required, `web` and `api` checks required, no force pushes
- PR "Ship it" merged through the rules

### Step by step
1. Add the `api` job next to Thursday's `web` job; they run in parallel.
2. Exclude migrations from coverage as in week 11.
3. Add the .NET threshold and check it fails when you lower the number on purpose.
4. Add Vitest thresholds the same way.
5. Create the ruleset in the repository settings and select both checks.
6. Run all builds and tests, push, review and merge PR "Ship it" through the ruleset.

```yaml
api:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  defaults: { run: { working-directory: api } }
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    # TODO: setup-dotnet, restore with cache, test with coverage, threshold
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Both jobs run on every pull request
- [ ] Each fails below its coverage threshold
- [ ] main cannot be changed without green checks
- [ ] PR "Ship it" is merged

### Hints
- Set thresholds slightly below today's numbers so they stop regressions without blocking you.
- Upload coverage reports as artifacts so reviewers can see what changed.

### Common mistakes
- Thresholds at 100%, so people write empty tests.
- Required checks with names that do not match the job names.

### Check your understanding
- What does a required check guarantee?
- Why thresholds below current coverage?
- Why run the API and web jobs in parallel?

days.title: Explain why the API must be stateless to scale out, with JobHunt examples, and write a multi-stage Dockerfile from memory
days.brief:
### The drill
Explain why the API must be stateless to scale out, with JobHunt examples, then write a multi-stage Dockerfile from memory, in 25 minutes.

### Rules
- Part 1 (about 10 minutes): blank page, explain out loud as if to an interviewer.
- Part 2 (about 15 minutes): a new empty folder outside the JobHunt repo with `dotnet new web`, then a Dockerfile written without looking at JobHunt's.
- Docs allowed, but try without first and note every lookup. No AI assistants.

### Must include
- Part 1: what goes wrong with two instances and in-memory state: SignalR groups, output cache eviction, Data Protection keys, files on local disk
- The fix for each: backplane, Redis output cache store, shared keys, blob storage
- What JobHunt accepts as per instance (rate limit counters, the event sequencer) and why that is fine
- Part 2: a build stage from the SDK image restoring before copying the source, a publish step, a final stage from the ASP.NET Core runtime image copying only the output
- A non-root user and port 8080
- A `.dockerignore`, and the image running with one setting from an environment variable

### Self-check
- [ ] Finished within 25 minutes
- [ ] Named four kinds of state and their fixes
- [ ] The image builds and answers a request
- [ ] Restore is cached when only code changes
- [ ] Explained why migrations run as a separate step
- [ ] Zero lookups, or a list of exactly what to review

### If you got stuck
- API Dockerfile: Monday, .NET part. Compose: Tuesday, .NET part.
- Migrations on deploy: Wednesday, .NET part. Scaling out: Thursday, .NET part.
- nginx and the SPA: Monday and Tuesday, React part. Runtime config: Wednesday, React part.
- CI: Thursday and Friday, React part. CD: Friday, .NET part.
